# The same physical laws on earth and in the heavens (`universal_physical_laws`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by telescope, universal_gravitation, falling_bodies, mathematical_laws_of_nature
- Core idea: The stars, planets and moon are made of ordinary matter and obey the same rules as stones and water here; there is no separate perfect, unchanging celestial realm. Evidence in rising order of force: new stars and comets show the heavens change (Tycho found their parallax too small for them to be atmospheric phenomena below the moon); a modest telescope shows mountains and shadows on the moon and spots on the sun; and the moon's orbit fits the same gravity that pulls an apple, weakened by the square of the distance (the moon is 60 earth radii away and falls 1/3600 as far per second as a stone does here). The pay-off is that experiments done on a bench tell us about the whole universe.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming the earth-heaven divide was a religious dogma; it was Aristotle's physics, with good arguments, and Chinese cosmology never had it
  - Saying the Church forbade the idea that the heavens change; Jesuit astronomers confirmed Galileo's observations within a year
  - Offering the moon-and-apple calculation without the earth's size and the moon's distance, both of which the listener must accept first
  - Suggesting the sun is a burning stone to a society that worships it; Anaxagoras was prosecuted for impiety in Athens for that
- History: greece: c. 450 BC – Anaxagoras: the sun is a glowing stone and the moon is earthy; c. 350 BC Aristotle fixes the opposite view of a fifth, unchanging celestial element; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus of Alexandria argues that the heavens are made of ordinary, perishable matter; china: from 28 BC – court astronomers record sunspots, and 'guest stars' throughout; the heavens were never assumed changeless; islamic: c. 1000 – al-Biruni questions Aristotle's celestial physics in his correspondence with Ibn Sina; europe: 1572–1577 – Tycho's nova and comet; 1610 Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius; 1687 Newton unites celestial and terrestrial mechanics; 1859–1860 Kirchhoff and Bunsen find terrestrial elements in the sun's spectrum
- Read:
  - Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (1610)
  - Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687)
  - Thomas S. Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution (1957)
